claim: Voltage-dependent Ca2+ channels (Cavs) are indispensable for coupling action potentials with Ca2+ signaling in living organisms.
source: Voltage-dependent Ca2+ channels (Cavs), which couple the membrane voltage with Ca2+ signaling, regulate some important physiological functions, such as neurotransmission and muscle contraction (Hille, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hille, 2001

claim: The channel subunits of both mammalian Cavs and mammalian voltage-dependent Na+ channels (Navs) have 24 transmembrane helices (24TM).
source: The channel subunits of both mammalian Cavs and mammalian voltage-dependent Na+ channels (Navs) have 24 transmembrane helices (24TM) (Catterall, 2000)
evidence: Supported by citation to Catterall, 2000

claim: Mammalian Cavs and Navs comprise four homologous subdomains with six transmembrane helices that correspond to one subunit of homo-tetrameric channels.
source: The channel subunits of both mammalian Cavs and mammalian voltage-dependent Na+ channels (Navs) have 24 transmembrane helices (24TM) (Catterall, 2000), and comprise four homologous subdomains with six transmembrane helices that correspond to one subunit of homo-tetrameric channels, such as voltage-dependent K+ channels and prokaryotic Navs (BacNavs).
evidence: Supported by citation to Catterall, 2000 and established knowledge of channel structure

claim: Comparison of the sequences of Navs and Cavs indicate that Navs derived from Cavs.
source: Comparison of the sequences of Navs and Cavs indicate that Navs derived from Cavs.
evidence: Inferred from sequence comparison analysis

claim: The two pairs of subdomains in Navs and Cavs (domains I and III, and domains II and IV) are evolutionarily close to each other.
source: Their two pairs of subdomains, domains I and III, and domains II and IV, are evolutionarily close to each other (Rahman et al., 2014; Strong et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rahman et al., 2014 and Strong et al., 1993

claim: The 24TM-type of Cavs are thought to have evolved from the single-domain type of Cavs with two domain-duplication events.
source: Therefore, the 24TM-type of Cavs are thought to have evolved from the single-domain type of Cavs with two domain-duplication events.
evidence: Inferred from evolutionary analysis of channel structure

claim: Native prokaryotic Cavs have not yet been identified prior to this study.
source: Although prokaryotes are expected to have such ancestor-like channels, native prokaryotic Cavs have not yet been identified.
evidence: Statement of the gap in knowledge prior to this study

claim: The lack of ancestor-like prokaryotic Cavs is a missing link in the evolution of voltage-dependent cation channels.
source: The lack of ancestor-like prokaryotic Cavs is a missing link in the evolution of voltage-dependent cation channels.
evidence: Inference based on evolutionary theory

claim: Many BacNavs have been characterized.
source: In contrast to the lack of prokaryotic Cavs, many BacNavs have been characterized (Irie et al., 2010; Ito et al., 2004; Koishi et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2012; Nagura et al., 2010; Payandeh et al., 2011; Ren et al., 2001; Shimomura et al., 2016; Shimomura et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The simple structure of BacNavs has helped to elucidate the molecular mechanisms of Navs.
source: The simple structure of BacNavs has helped to elucidate the molecular mechanisms of Navs (Irie et al., 2018; Irie et al., 2012; Tsai et al., 2013; Yue et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: BacNavs have been used as a genetic tool for manipulating neuronal excitability in vivo.
source: In addition, BacNavs have been used as a genetic tool for manipulating neuronal excitability in vivo (Bando et al., 2016; Kamiya et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies demonstrating this application

claim: The acquisition of Ca2+ selectivity by BacNavs can be engineered by the introduction of several negatively charged amino acids into the selectivity filter.
source: The acquisition of Ca2+ selectivity by BacNavs can be engineered by the introduction of several negatively charged amino acids into the selectivity filter (Tang et al., 2014; Yue et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tang et al., 2014 and Yue et al., 2002

claim: A mutant channel NavAb with introduced negatively charged residues showed high Ca2+ selectivity.
source: A mutant channel NavAb (a BacNav from Arcobacter butzleri) produced in this way, showed high Ca2+ selectivity, and the structural basis of Ca2+ selectivity has been discussed on the basis of its crystal structures (Tang et al., 2016; Tang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tang et al., 2016 and Tang et al., 2014

claim: The selectivity filter sequences of CavAb are quite different from those of the original mammalian Cavs.
source: However, the selectivity filter sequences of CavAb, which were made by mutation of NavAb and contain a large number of aspartates, are quite different from those of the original mammalian Cavs.
evidence: Comparison of sequences between CavAb and mammalian Cavs

claim: BacNavs acquired sodium selectivity independent from that of 24TM Navs.
source: The evolutional analysis also indicated that BacNavs acquired sodium selectivity independent from that of 24TM Navs (Liebeskind et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liebeskind et al., 2013

claim: CavMr from Meiothermus ruber and NavPp from Plesiocystis pacifica are two newly characterized BacNav homologs.
source: Here, we newly characterized two BacNav homologs, CavMr from Meiothermus ruber and NavPp from Plesiocystis pacifica.
evidence: Direct statement of the study's findings

claim: CavMr and NavPp are evolutionarily distant from the previously reported canonical BacNavs.
source: These two channels are evolutionarily distant from the previously reported canonical BacNavs.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis presented in the study

claim: CavMr has clear Ca2+ selectivity.
source: We confirmed that CavMr has clear Ca2+ selectivity, and that NavPp has Na+ selectivity with Ca2+-dependent inhibition.
evidence: Based on electrophysiological measurements in the study

claim: NavPp has Na+ selectivity with Ca2+-dependent inhibition.
source: We confirmed that CavMr has clear Ca2+ selectivity, and that NavPp has Na+ selectivity with Ca2+-dependent inhibition.
evidence: Based on electrophysiological measurements in the study

claim: The glycine residue of the CavMr selectivity filter is a determinant for Ca2+ selectivity.
source: Mutational analyses revealed that the glycine residue of the CavMr selectivity filter is a determinant for Ca2+ selectivity.
evidence: Based on mutational analysis data presented in the study

claim: The glycine residue at position 4 is well conserved among subdomains I and III of eukaryotic Cavs.
source: This glycine residue is well conserved among subdomains I and III of eukaryotic Cavs.
evidence: Based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1a

claim: In mammalian and prokaryotic Navs and Cavs, a larger number of negative charges in the filter increases Ca2+ selectivity.
source: In mammalian and prokaryotic Navs and Cavs, a larger number of negative charges in the filter increases Ca2+ selectivity (Figure 1a) (Heinemann et al., 1992; Tang et al., 2014; Yue et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1a

claim: Several BLAST search rounds using the pore regions (S5–S6) of NaChBac as templates revealed a series of candidate prokaryotic Cavs whose selectivity filters are similar to the 'TLESW' motif.
source: Several BLAST search rounds using the pore regions (S5–S6) of NaChBac (or NavBh; a BacNav from Bacillus halodurans) as templates revealed a series of candidate prokaryotic Cavs whose selectivity filters are similar to the 'TLESW' motif, but which contain more negatively charged residues like the filter sequence of CavAb (Figure 1a).
evidence: Based on BLAST search methodology and results shown in Figure 1a

claim: Phylogenetic analysis revealed that the candidate prokaryotic Cavs belong to a different branch of the tree than that of canonical BacNavs.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of these channel genes revealed that they apparently belong to a different branch of the tree than that of canonical BacNavs, namely a Bacillus group and a NavAb-like group (Figure 1b; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1b

claim: The selectivity filter sequences of the newly identified channels are similar to that of the ancestral BacNav channel predicted previously.
source: The selectivity filter sequences of these channels are similar to that of the ancestral BacNav channel predicted previously (Liebeskind et al., 2013).
evidence: Comparison with predictions from Liebeskind et al., 2013

claim: The newly identified channels are named ancestor-like BacNavs (AnclNavs).
source: Therefore, we named these channels ancestor-like BacNavs (AnclNavs).
evidence: Nomenclature decision based on phylogenetic analysis

claim: AnclNavs are widely distributed in multiple bacterial phyla and even in archaea.
source: AnclNavs are widely distributed in multiple bacterial phyla and even in archaea (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic distribution analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The firmicutes phylum contains neither homologs of NavAb-like BacNavs nor homologs of AnclNavs.
source: In addition, the firmicutes phylum, which includes Bacillus species, contains neither homologs of NavAb-like BacNavs nor homologs of AnclNavs.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis of bacterial species

claim: AnclNavs are homologs rather than orthologs of canonical BacNavs and compose a distinct group.
source: These observations suggest that our identified candidate prokaryotic Cavs, AnclNavs, are homologs rather than orthologs of canonical BacNavs and compose a distinct group.
evidence: Inference from phylogenetic analysis

claim: Phylogenetic analyses that include eukaryotic channels put AnclNavs closest to a Bacillus group.
source: In addition, analyses that include some eukaryotic channels, such as each subdomain of 24TM-type of Navs/Cavs, CatSper and EukCatA, a group of eukaryotic non-selective homotetrameric channels, put AnclNavs closest to a Bacillus group (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Figure 1—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Four AnclNavs genes were identified and their channel activity was measured.
source: We identified four AnclNavs genes and measured their channel activity: ZP_04038264 from M. ruber, ZP_01909854 from P. pacifica, YP 003896792_from Halomonas elongata, and YP_003073405 from Teredinibacter turnerae (Figure 1b and c).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental approach

claim: Insect cells are often better than mammalian cells for generating large current amplitudes when expressing prokaryotic channels transgenetically.
source: When attempting to express prokaryotic channels transgenetically, insect cells are often better than mammalian cells for generating large current amplitudes (Irie et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Irie et al., 2018

claim: Sf9 cells transfected with the M. ruber gene showed currents in response to a depolarizing stimulus from a −140 mV holding potential.
source: The cells that were transfected with genes from M. ruber showed currents in response to a depolarizing stimulus from a −140 mV holding potential (Figure 2a).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2a

claim: The M. ruber channel had larger currents in the high-Ca2+ solution than in the high-Na+ solution.
source: The M. ruber channel clearly had larger currents in the high-Ca2+ solution than in the high-Na+ solution, and no obvious outward current was observed in a high-Ca2+ bath solution, even at very high membrane potential (100 mV) (Figure 2a and b; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Based on current-voltage relationship measurements shown in Figure 2a and b

claim: No obvious outward current was observed in the M. ruber channel in a high-Ca2+ bath solution, even at very high membrane potential (100 mV).
source: The M. ruber channel clearly had larger currents in the high-Ca2+ solution than in the high-Na+ solution, and no obvious outward current was observed in a high-Ca2+ bath solution, even at very high membrane potential (100 mV) (Figure 2a and b; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Based on current-voltage relationship measurements shown in Figure 2a and b

claim: The current-voltage relationships of the M. ruber channel suggest that it has a preference for Ca2+.
source: These current-voltage relationships suggest that the M. ruber channel has a preference for Ca2+, and that other cations inside the cells (sodium and cesium) hardly permeated the activated channel.
evidence: Inference from current-voltage relationship data

claim: Other cations inside the cells (sodium and cesium) hardly permeated the activated M. ruber channel.
source: These current-voltage relationships suggest that the M. ruber channel has a preference for Ca2+, and that other cations inside the cells (sodium and cesium) hardly permeated the activated channel.
evidence: Inference from current-voltage relationship data

claim: A Boltzmann fit of the averaged activation curve of CavMr yielded a V1/2 of −51.7 ± 1.1 mV.
source: A Boltzmann fit of the averaged activation curve yielded an activating potential of 50% activation (V1/2) of −51.7 ± 1.1 mV (Figure 2d; Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: Based on analysis of deactivation tail currents shown in Figure 2c and d

claim: The amino acid sequence of the selectivity filter in CavMr is similar to the conserved features of domains I/III in mammalian Cavs.
source: Notably, the amino acid sequence of the selectivity filter in CavMr is similar to the conserved features of domains I/III in mammalian Cavs, with a glycine at position 4 and a polar or negatively charged residue at position 7, which are not observed in the canonical BacNav family.
evidence: Based on sequence comparison analysis

claim: The CavMr selectivity filter has a glycine at position 4 and a polar or negatively charged residue at position 7, which are not observed in the canonical BacNav family.
source: Notably, the amino acid sequence of the selectivity filter in CavMr is similar to the conserved features of domains I/III in mammalian Cavs, with a glycine at position 4 and a polar or negatively charged residue at position 7, which are not observed in the canonical BacNav family.
evidence: Based on sequence comparison analysis

claim: The CavMr selectivity filter sequence is very similar to that of the human Cav subdomain I.
source: In addition, the CavMr selectivity filter sequence is quite similar to that of the human Cav subdomain I, or even the same as Cav3.1 and 3.2 (Figure 1a).
evidence: Based on sequence comparison shown in Figure 1a

claim: The CavMr selectivity filter sequence is the same as human Cav3.1 and 3.2 subdomain I.
source: In addition, the CavMr selectivity filter sequence is quite similar to that of the human Cav subdomain I, or even the same as Cav3.1 and 3.2 (Figure 1a).
evidence: Based on sequence comparison shown in Figure 1a

claim: T220A and G229A mutations in NaChBac led to slower inactivation and provided a larger current.
source: T220A and G229A mutations in NaChBac led to slower inactivation and provided a larger current, indicating suppression of the transition to the inactivated state (Irie et al., 2010; Shimomura et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Irie et al., 2010 and Shimomura et al., 2016

claim: The G240A mutant of CavMr stably showed larger and more measurable currents than the wild-type channel.
source: Th is mutant channels stably showed larger and more measurable currents than the wild-type channel, even after they were administrated multiple depolarizing stimuli (Figure 2e and f).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2e and f

claim: The plot of the reversal potentials of CavMr as a function of [Ca2+]out had a slope of 39.89 ± 3.31 mV/decade.
source: The plot of the reversal potentials as a function of [Ca2+]out had a slope of 39.89 ± 3.31 mV/decade (n = 4).
evidence: Based on reversal potential measurements under bi-ionic conditions

claim: The slope of reversal potentials for CavMr was higher than the Nernst prediction for a divalent cation (29 mV).
source: It was higher than the Nernst prediction for a divalent cation (29 mV).
evidence: Comparison with theoretical Nernst equation prediction

claim: The plot of the reversal potentials in 4, 10 and 20 mM Ca2+ bath solutions as a function of [Ca2+]out had a slope of 32.38 ± 4.10 mV/decade.
source: The well-fitted plot of the reversal potentials in 4, 10 and 20 mM Ca2+ bath solutions as a function of [Ca2+]outdid indeed have a slope of 32.38 ± 4.10 mV/decade (n = 4) (Figure 3b dashed line), a value close to the Nernst equation for Ca2+ (Figure 3b)
evidence: Based on reversal potential measurements shown in Figure 3b

claim: CavMr had a PCa/PNa of 218 ± 38.
source: and indicated that CavMr had a PCa/PNa of 218 ± 38 (Figure 3e, Table 1; Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: Based on reversal potential measurements and GHK equation calculations shown in Figure 3e and Table 1

claim: The PCa/PNa value of CavMr is comparable to that of CavAb.
source: This high PCa/PNa value is comparable to that of CavAb.
evidence: Comparison with previously reported CavAb data

claim: Among several species of cations, including Sr2+, K+, and Cs+, Ca2+ had the highest permeability relative to Na+ in CavMr.
source: Among several species of cations, including Sr2+, K+, and Cs+, Ca2+ had the highest permeability relative to Na+ (Figure 3c,d and f, Table 1; Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: Based on ion selectivity measurements shown in Figure 3c, d, f and Table 1

claim: CavMr is a native prokaryotic Cav with high Ca2+ selectivity.
source: On the basis of these results, CavMr was confirmed to be a native prokaryotic Cav with high Ca2+ selectivity.
evidence: Conclusion based on ion selectivity measurements

claim: CavMr did not allow Na+ permeation under Ca2+-free (0 mM CaCl2 and 1 mM EGTA) conditions.
source: CavMr did not allow Na+ permeation under Ca2+-free (0 mM CaCl2 and 1 mM EGTA) conditions (Figure 4a and b; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4a and b

claim: CavMr did not show the typical anomalous mole fraction effect.
source: CavMr did not allow Na+ permeation under Ca2+-free (0 mM CaCl2 and 1 mM EGTA) conditions (Figure 4a and b; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Based on mole fraction effect experiments shown in Figure 4a and b

claim: CavMr had an apparently monotonic current increase depending on the Ca2+ mole fraction to Na+.
source: Also, in contrast to the recording of NaChBac currents in a solution containing Na+ and K+, CavMr had an apparently monotonic current increase depending on the Ca2+ mole fraction to Na+ (Figure 4c and d; Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: Based on mole fraction effect experiments shown in Figure 4c and d

claim: The currents derived from the P. pacifica channel became large with increases in the bath Na+ concentration.
source: The currents derived from the P. pacifica channel became large with increases in the bath Na+ concentration and significantly decreased when the Na+ solution was replaced with a high Ca2+ solution (Figure 5a and b; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5a and b

claim: The currents from the P. pacifica channel significantly decreased when the Na+ solution was replaced with a high Ca2+ solution.
source: The currents derived from the P. pacifica channel became large with increases in the bath Na+ concentration and significantly decreased when the Na+ solution was replaced with a high Ca2+ solution (Figure 5a and b; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5a and b

claim: The reversal potential of NavPp fit well to the Na+ equilibrium potential in the high-Na+ solution.
source: Because the reversal potential fit well to the Na+ equilibrium potential in the high-Na+ solution (Figure 5b), we abbreviated this channel as NavPp on the basis of its ion selectivity and species name.
evidence: Based on reversal potential measurements shown in Figure 5b

claim: NavPp, despite having one more aspartate in the selectivity filter than CavMr, exhibited larger currents in Na+ solutions than in Ca2+ solutions.
source: Interestingly, NavPp, despite having one more aspartate in the selectivity filter than CavMr, exhibited larger currents in Na+ solutions than in Ca2+ solutions (Figure 1c and Figure 5a).
evidence: Based on comparison of selectivity filter sequences and electrophysiological data

claim: Ca2+ selection is not achieved simply by increasing negative charges in the filter sequence of the AnclNav group.
source: This observation indicates that Ca2+ selection is not achieved simply by increasing negative charges in the filter sequence of the AnclNav group, which again suggests the existence of an alternative ion-selectivity mechanism.
evidence: Inference from comparison of CavMr and NavPp properties

claim: Recordings in bath solution containing both Na+ and Ca2+ demonstrated that the increment of the extracellular Ca2+ decreased the current in NavPp.
source: Recordings in bath solution containing both Na+ and Ca2+ demonstrated that the increment of the extracellular Ca2+ decreased the current in NavPp and led to a positive shift in the voltage dependence, suggesting that a higher concentration of Ca2+ inhibited the gating and ionic permeation of NavPp (Figure 5b).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5b

claim: The increment of extracellular Ca2+ led to a positive shift in the voltage dependence of NavPp.
source: Recordings in bath solution containing both Na+ and Ca2+ demonstrated that the increment of the extracellular Ca2+ decreased the current in NavPp and led to a positive shift in the voltage dependence, suggesting that a higher concentration of Ca2+ inhibited the gating and ionic permeation of NavPp (Figure 5b).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5b

claim: A higher concentration of Ca2+ inhibited the gating and ionic permeation of NavPp.
source: Recordings in bath solution containing both Na+ and Ca2+ demonstrated that the increment of the extracellular Ca2+ decreased the current in NavPp and led to a positive shift in the voltage dependence, suggesting that a higher concentration of Ca2+ inhibited the gating and ionic permeation of NavPp (Figure 5b).
evidence: Inference from electrophysiological recordings

claim: Wild-type NavPp showed very fast deactivation and no tail current was observed.
source: We tried to measure the voltage-dependent activation of NavPp, but the wild-type channel showed very fast deactivation and no tail current was observed (Figure 5c).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5c

claim: The NavPp T232A mutant allowed observation of tail current at −60 mV.
source: By introducing a T232A mutation, corresponding to the NaChBac mutations of T220A (Shimomura et al., 2016), we were able to observe the tail current at −60 mV (Figure 5d and e).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5d and e

claim: A Boltzmann fit of the averaged activation curve of NavPp T232A yielded a V1/2 of −17.11 ± 1.8 mV.
source: A Boltzmann fit of the averaged activation curve of NavPp T232A yielded a V1/2 of −17.11 ± 1.8 mV (Figure 5f; Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: Based on analysis of tail currents shown in Figure 5f

claim: The increments of the extracellular Ca2+ raised the value of the reversal potential in NavPp.
source: The increments of the extracellular Ca2+ raised the value of the reversal potential, indicating that extracellular calcium ions can also permeate NavPp (Figure 6b).
evidence: Based on reversal potential measurements shown in Figure 6b

claim: Extracellular calcium ions can permeate NavPp.
source: The increments of the extracellular Ca2+ raised the value of the reversal potential, indicating that extracellular calcium ions can also permeate NavPp (Figure 6b).
evidence: Inference from reversal potential measurements

claim: In higher extracellular Ca2+ concentrations, the current amplitude of NavPp became smaller, even in the voltage at which NavPp opens fully.
source: However, in higher extracellular Ca2+ concentrations, the current amplitude of NavPp became smaller, even in the voltage at which NavPp opens fully, and the voltage dependence of the activation shifted more positively (Figure 6b–c).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6b-c

claim: The voltage dependence of the activation of NavPp shifted more positively in higher extracellular Ca2+ concentrations.
source: However, in higher extracellular Ca2+ concentrations, the current amplitude of NavPp became smaller, even in the voltage at which NavPp opens fully, and the voltage dependence of the activation shifted more positively (Figure 6b–c).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 6b-c

claim: Calcium ions can permeate NavPp but disturb the gating and ionic permeation of NavPp.
source: These results indicated that calcium ions can permeate NavPp but disturb the gating and ionic permeation of NavPp.
evidence: Inference from electrophysiological data on Ca2+ effects

claim: The selectivity of NavPp was higher for Na+ than for Ca2+, Sr2+, K+, or Cs+.
source: The selectivity of NavPp was higher for Na+ than for Ca2+, Sr2+, K+, or Cs+ (Figure 6d and e; Figure 6—source data 3).

claim: The PCa/PNa of NavPp was 0.308 ± 0.028 in a bath solution containing both Ca2+ and Na+.
source: The PCa/PNa was 0.308 ± 0.028 in a bath solution containing both Ca2+ and Na+, suggesting that a larger fraction of Ca2+ is allowed to permeate with outside Na+ ions through NavPp than through canonical BacNavs.
evidence: Based on reversal potential measurements and GHK equation calculations

claim: A larger fraction of Ca2+ is allowed to permeate with outside Na+ ions through NavPp than through canonical BacNavs.
source: The PCa/PNa was 0.308 ± 0.028 in a bath solution containing both Ca2+ and Na+, suggesting that a larger fraction of Ca2+ is allowed to permeate with outside Na+ ions through NavPp than through canonical BacNavs.
evidence: Inference from PCa/PNa measurements

claim: Sr2+ also blocked the NavPp current, but may also permeate the channel along with Na+ ions.

claim: NavPp demonstrates a unique feature of low-affinity Ca2+ block, which is not reported in canonical BacNavs.
source: These findings demonstrate a unique feature of NavPp, a low-affinity Ca2+ block, which is not reported in canonical BacNavs.
evidence: Inference from comparison with canonical BacNavs

claim: The filter sequence of NavPp has three negatively charged residues, similar to the filter sequences of the artificial Ca2+-selective BacNav mutants.
source: Interestingly, the filter sequence of NavPp, 'TLEDWTD', has three negatively charged residues, similar to the filter sequences of the artificial Ca2+-selective BacNav mutants (the 'TLEDWSD' mutant of NavAb and the 'TLEDWAD' mutant of NaChBac) (Tang et al., 2014; Yue et al., 2002).

claim: NavPp does not show high Ca2+ permeability, but rather a Ca2+ block.

claim: NavPp-T6A showed no inward current in bath solutions containing divalent cations.

claim: Both of the selectivity filter sequences that provide Ca2+ selectivity to canonical BacNavs failed to generate Ca2+-permeable NavPp.

claim: The cation-permeable mechanism of NavPp differs from that of canonical BacNavs, as well as that of CavMr.

claim: Cells transfected with genes from H. elongata and T. turnerae failed to show any detectable currents.

claim: NavPp-Mr exhibited high Sr2+ selectivity, comparable to that of CavMr.

claim: NavPp-Mr excluded Na+ and K+ similar to CavMr, but weakly allowed Cs+ permeation in contrast to CavMr.

claim: CavMr and NavAb achieve cation selectivity using different structural backbones and mechanisms.
